subskill: recognizing the two triangles of an SSA configuration and finding the gap between the two possible third sides
prompt: In triangle ABC, AB = 10, BC = 7, and the measure of angle A is 37°. Exactly two noncongruent triangles satisfy these conditions. To the nearest hundredth, what is the positive difference between the two possible lengths of side AC ?

Because BH < BC = 7 < AB, point C can sit on either side of H with HC = √(7² − BH²) ≈ √(49 − 36.22) ≈ 3.575. The two possible lengths are AH + HC ≈ 11.56 and AH − HC ≈ 4.41, so their difference is 2·HC ≈ 7.15. (Equivalently, the law of cosines gives AC² − 2(10 cos 37°)AC + (100 − 49) = 0, whose roots differ by the square root of the discriminant, ≈ 7.15.) The option "4.41" is the shorter possible length of AC, reported instead of the difference. The option "6.02" is BH, the altitude that decides whether the case is ambiguous. The option "1.96" finds HC by subtracting, HC = BC − BH = 7 − 6.018, instead of using the Pythagorean theorem, and doubles that.

The option "4.93" takes the altitude to the hypotenuse to be √(6·11), the geometric mean of the legs, instead of 6·11/√157.
